title: Karnaugh Maps & Minimization
summary: A K-map turns boolean minimization into a visual pattern-matching game — powerful by hand for a handful of variables, before an algorithmic method takes over at scale.

slides.markdown:
A raw sum-of-products expression straight off a truth table is usually far from minimal — it has one term per true row, with lots of redundancy between them. **Minimizing** it to fewer, shorter terms translates directly into **fewer gates and shorter critical paths** once built in hardware.

Fewer gates means less silicon area, less power draw, and (from the previous topic's gate-delay lesson) a shorter propagation chain — minimization isn't an academic exercise, it's a direct cost reduction on a real chip.

slides.subTitle: Gray-code adjacency
slides.markdown:
A **Karnaugh map (K-map)** arranges a truth table's outputs in a grid where **row and column labels change by only one bit between adjacent cells** — this ordering is called **Gray code** (unlike counting in plain binary, where multiple bits can flip at once).

That single-bit-change property is the whole trick: any two **physically adjacent** cells in the grid differ in exactly one input variable, so a group of adjacent `1`s reveals a term where that differing variable has simply dropped out.

slides.subTitle: 4-variable K-map with groupings
slides.markdown:
A 4-variable K-map is a 4x4 grid (16 cells), with groups of adjacent 1s circled to find minimal terms:

![A 4-variable K-map with two groups circled, one an 8-cell group and one a 4-cell group](assets/kmap-4var-grouping.svg)

The large 8-cell group spans half the map and eliminates 3 of the 4 variables, leaving a single-literal term. The smaller 4-cell group eliminates 2 variables. Reading each circled group off the map — instead of reasoning about the raw truth table — is the entire K-map method in miniature.

assets.alt: A 4-variable K-map with two groups circled, one an 8-cell group and one a 4-cell group

slides.subTitle: Powers of two, overlaps, don't-cares
slides.markdown:
Valid groups follow strict rules:

- **Size must be a power of two** — 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 cells; never 3, 5, 6.
- **Groups can overlap** — the same `1` cell can belong to multiple groups if that makes each group larger.
- **Bigger is always better** — a bigger group eliminates more variables; prefer the largest valid group covering a cell.
- **Don't-cares (`X`)** — inputs that can never occur can be treated as either 0 or 1, whichever forms a bigger group.

The goal each pass: cover every `1` with the fewest, largest groups.

slides.subTitle: Reading off the minimized expression
slides.markdown:
Once groups are circled, each group becomes **one AND term** in the final sum-of-products: keep only the variables that stay **constant** across every cell in that group (drop any variable that changes value within the group, since a group spans both its states).

OR all the group-terms together for the final minimized expression. A group spanning all 16 cells of a 4-variable map, for instance, would drop every variable and reduce to the constant `1` — the function is always true.

slides.subTitle: K-maps vs Quine-McCluskey
slides.markdown:
K-maps are a **visual, manual** method; **Quine-McCluskey** is the equivalent **algorithmic, tabular** method that scales to more variables:

| | K-maps | Quine-McCluskey |
|---|---|---|
| Practical limit | ~4-6 variables (visual grouping breaks down beyond that) | Any number of variables (systematic table comparison) |
| Method | Visually group adjacent 1s by inspection | Iteratively combine terms differing in one bit, tabulated |
| Who uses it | Students, quick manual designs | EDA tools, automated logic synthesis |

Real chip design tools use Quine-McCluskey (or more advanced variants) precisely because a real circuit can easily have dozens of input variables — far past where a human can visually group a K-map.

slides.subTitle: Missing wrap-around adjacency
slides.markdown:
The K-map grid **wraps around** — the leftmost column is adjacent to the rightmost column, and the top row is adjacent to the bottom row, because Gray-code labeling continues cyclically. Visually, the map is really drawn on a torus, not a flat rectangle.

A common beginner mistake is only grouping cells that look adjacent on the flat page and missing a legal group that wraps from one edge to the opposite edge — leading to a larger (non-minimal) final expression than necessary. Always explicitly check the four edges against their opposite edges before finalizing groups.
